key_terms.meaning: Mass of air entering the engine ÷ mass of fuel metered; petrol engines run near 14.7:1 at stoichiometric and need about 12:1 for full power.
The narrowed throat in a carburettor where air speeds up, static pressure falls, and fuel is drawn out of the main jet.
Fuel path that feeds a rich mixture through a small port just below the closed throttle plate, where venturi suction is too weak.
Extra enrichment device, a metering rod or power valve, that adds fuel only at high load so cruise stays lean and full load rich.
Small plunger linked to the throttle that squirts a shot of neat fuel when the throttle is snapped open, covering the brief lean patch.
Fuel is injected into the intake port or a pre-chamber, not straight into the cylinder, so it mixes with air before entering.
Inline plunger-and-barrel pump driven by a cam; delivery starts when the plunger covers the inlet port and ends when its helical edge uncovers the spill port.
Pump and nozzle built as one body at each cylinder, so pressure is made close to the nozzle with no long high-pressure pipe.
One thick tube kept full of fuel at high pressure by a separate pump; each injector is opened electrically, so rail pressure and timing are set independently.
One solenoid injector per cylinder spraying into the intake port just upstream of the inlet valve.
Petrol sprayed at high pressure straight into the cylinder, allowing a stratified lean charge near the plug at part load.
Breaking a liquid jet into fine droplets, which multiplies surface area so the fuel evaporates and mixes with air quickly.
Diameter of the drop whose volume-to-surface ratio equals that of the whole spray; a smaller SMD means a finer spray.
Distance the spray tip travels from the nozzle before air drag stops it; it must reach across the chamber without hitting the wall as a liquid.
Full included angle of the spray leaving the nozzle, fixed by hole geometry and reduced by higher air density in the cylinder.
Nozzle with a pin (pintle) through the hole that gives a hollow-cone spray and a large flow area, used where choking is a risk at low speed.
Nozzle with several small holes, giving fine atomisation and one spray jet aimed at each air stream in the combustion chamber.
Device that senses engine speed and moves the fuel rack or control lever to hold a set speed as load changes.
Self-contained ignition unit with its own rotating magnet and coil, generating the spark without any battery supply.
Crank angle before top dead centre at which the spark fires; it must increase with speed and decrease with load.

takeaways: A carburettor cannot meet all demands with one fuel passage, so separate idle, main, power and acceleration circuits switch in as airflow rises.
A fuel injection system must meter, atomise, distribute and time the fuel; the pump only pressurises and times, the nozzle does the atomising.
In a jerk pump the helical control edge on the plunger sets the delivered quantity by deciding when spill begins.
Common rail separates pressure generation from injection, so injection pressure can be chosen for each operating point, and split injections become possible.
Electronic fuel injection replaced mechanical metering because the ECU can hold the air-fuel ratio close to target from cold start to full load.
Nozzle hole size and number trade atomisation against penetration; small holes atomise well but penetrate poorly, which matters in a deep bowl.
A governor is a closed-loop speed controller: it compares actual speed with the set speed and corrects the fuel rack, always with some droop.
Battery-coil ignition gets its energy from the battery, magneto ignition makes its own; both rely on the collapsing field of an induction coil.
Spark advance is scheduled so peak cylinder pressure lands near 10–15° after TDC; too much advance and too slow a flame both lead to knock.
bank_note: Long answers usually pair a labelled sketch with the reason for each feature: mixture curves for carburettors, pump-and-nozzle timing diagrams for diesel, and advance curves for ignition.

bank.q: Draw the mixture requirement curve of a petrol engine over its load range and explain why the carburettor needs separate idle, main, power and acceleration circuits.
outline: Curve: rich at idle, lean at cruise, rich at full load
Idle port below the throttle plate supplies fuel at low airflow
Main circuit with venturi and main jet works from part load upward
Economiser or metering rod enriches at high load
Accelerating pump gives a transient shot of fuel
Choke enriches for cold start and warm-up

bank.q: State the requirements of a fuel injection system and classify its types by air assist, by direct or indirect injection, and by control method.
outline: Requirements: correct quantity, correct timing, good atomisation, proper distribution, low cost and reliability
Air-assisted vs solid injection
Direct injection into the cylinder vs indirect injection into port or pre-chamber
Mechanical, electronic and common-rail control

bank.q: Explain the construction and working of a jerk-type inline fuel pump and a distributor pump, and state how each times delivery and ends it.
outline: Cam, roller tappet, plunger, barrel, inlet and spill ports
Start of delivery when plunger closes the inlet port
End of delivery when the helical edge uncovers the spill port
Rotation of the plunger changes the effective stroke and so the quantity
Distributor pump has one plunger feeding all cylinders through a rotary distributor
Phasing of camshaft to engine gives correct injection timing

bank.q: Describe common rail direct injection with a layout sketch and explain how rail pressure and injection timing are controlled independently.
outline: Low-pressure transfer pump, high-pressure pump with pressure control valve, rail, pressure sensor, injectors, ECU
Rail stores fuel at high pressure; pressure sensor closes the loop
Injector opens by solenoid or piezo signal from ECU
Pressure set by rail, timing and duration set by injector drive
Allows pilot, main and post injections
Benefits: better atomisation at low speed, lower noise and emissions

bank.q: Compare battery-coil and magneto ignition systems on energy source, main components, starting behaviour and typical application.
outline: Battery-coil: battery, switch, coil, contact breaker or electronic trigger, distributor, plugs
Magneto: rotating magnet, coil, breaker, no battery needed
Magneto output rises with speed; weak spark at cranking
Battery system gives good spark at low speed and is used in cars
Magneto is used where no battery exists, such as small engines and aircraft
Both depend on the collapsing primary field inducing a high secondary voltage

bank.q: A four-cylinder petrol engine is converted from a carburettor to multi-point electronic fuel injection. Describe the sensors, ECU inputs and injector drive that must be added, and sketch the system layout.
outline: Sensors: manifold absolute pressure or air flow, throttle position, coolant temperature, air temperature. crankshaft position, oxygen sensor
ECU computes mass airflow and target air-fuel ratio, then injector pulse width
Fuel pump, filter, rail, pressure regulator, one injector per port
Speed-density or mass-air control strategy
Closed-loop correction from the oxygen sensor
Benefits: precise ratio, better cold start, lower emissions

bank.q: Explain how hole diameter, number of holes and nozzle opening pressure change atomisation, penetration and cone angle, and use this to choose a nozzle for a small high-speed direct injection diesel with a deep bowl.
outline: Smaller holes give finer spray, smaller Sauter mean diameter, shorter penetration
More holes give better use of air but less penetration per jet and weaker structural strength
Higher opening and injection pressure raise velocity, reduce drop size, lengthen penetration
Higher air density shortens penetration and widens cone angle
For a deep bowl: small holes, higher injection pressure, number of holes matched to air motion
Avoid wall wetting, which causes smoke and oil dilution

bank.q: Explain how a mechanical centrifugal governor holds engine speed when load is suddenly removed, and define speed droop and the effect of the governor spring rate.
outline: Flyweights move out with speed and push the sleeve against the spring
Sleeve motion is linked to the fuel rack
Load removed, speed rises, flyweights move rack to cut fuel
Equilibrium only at a slightly different speed, which is droop
Stiffer spring means less droop but coarser control
Hunting if the response is too fast or too slow

bank.q: Sketch spark advance against engine speed at part load and at full load, and explain how centrifugal and vacuum advance mechanisms produce these curves.
outline: Advance increases roughly linearly with speed
Advance falls as load rises, that is, as manifold vacuum falls
Centrifugal advance: weights move with speed and rotate the breaker plate or reluctor
Vacuum advance: diaphragm senses manifold vacuum and adds advance at light load
Mechanical limits, then ECU map with knock sensor feedback
Reason: fixed burn duration in time needs more crank angle at higher speed

bank.q: Explain how injection pressure, cylinder air density and split injection each change spray behaviour and mixture formation in a diesel engine.
outline: Higher injection pressure gives higher velocity, finer drops, longer penetration
Higher air density gives more drag, shorter penetration, wider cone
Pilot injection starts a small premixed burn that shortens ignition delay of the main pulse
Post injection helps late oxidation and DPF regeneration
Better mixing lowers soot; lower peak temperature lowers NOx
Trade-off between smoke, NOx and fuel consumption

bank.q: A diesel truck blows black smoke and hunts at idle. Trace the fault through the fuel rack, governor and nozzle, and justify each check you would make.
outline: Black smoke means over-fuelling or poor mixing: check maximum fuel stop and rack setting
Governor hunting: check flyweights, spring, oil level and linkage play
Nozzle: opening pressure test, leak test, spray pattern and chatter
Clogged air filter gives rich mixture too, so check air side
Injection timing too retarded raises smoke
Order of checks from cheapest to most invasive

bank.q: Compare carburettor, multi-point injection and gasoline direct injection for fuel metering accuracy, mixture distribution between cylinders and part-load efficiency.
outline: Carburettor: simple, cheap, poor cylinder-to-cylinder distribution, no closed-loop control
MPFI: port injection, accurate pulse width, good distribution, closed loop with oxygen sensor, some wall wetting
GDI: stratified lean part load, charge cooling, higher compression ratio, but particulates and injector deposits
Emissions and cost comparison
Justified conclusion for a given duty

bank.q: Explain why a common rail system with split injection can reduce both NOx and smoke where a jerk pump cannot, using pressure-time and heat-release reasoning.
outline: Jerk pump pressure falls with speed and quantity, so atomisation is poor at low load
CRDI holds pressure independent of speed and quantity
Pilot injection cuts ignition delay and the premixed spike, lowering NOx and noise
Higher pressure gives better mixing and less soot
Multiple injections shape the heat release rate
Cost, complexity and calibration effort as the counter-argument

bank.q: Explain how spark timing that is too advanced causes knock in a spark ignition engine, and how the ECU uses a knock sensor to correct it.
outline: Early spark raises peak pressure and temperature before flame arrives
End gas is compressed and auto-ignites, giving knock
Too little advance loses power and overheats the exhaust
Knock sensor is a piezoelectric accelerometer on the block
ECU retards timing in steps and restores it slowly
Relation of advance to speed, load, fuel octane and coolant temperature

glossary.def: The chemically exact ratio at which fuel burns completely in air, about 14.7:1 by mass for petrol and 14.5:1 for diesel.
Small fuel bowl in a carburettor kept at constant level by a float and needle valve, so jet flow depends only on venturi suction.
Calibrated hole that limits fuel flow from the float chamber into the main well and venturi.
Butterfly above the venturi that is closed during cold starting to raise manifold vacuum and draw extra fuel.
Mono-point electronic injection with one or two injectors mounted above the throttle plate, replacing the carburettor.
Electrically or mechanically opened valve that delivers a metered, atomised charge of fuel.
Electronic control unit; the computer that reads sensors, calculates the fuel and spark demands, and drives the injectors and coil.
Short delay between the start of pump delivery and the moment the nozzle actually opens, caused by pressure-wave travel and nozzle opening pressure.
Non-return valve on a pump outlet that keeps the high-pressure pipe full and makes the pressure fall sharply at the end of injection.
Rotary diesel pump with one pumping plunger that sends fuel to each cylinder in turn through a rotating distributor head.
The pressure held in the common rail, measured by a sensor and held by a control valve; typically several hundred to over two thousand bar.
Injector opened by a stack of piezo crystals that expand when charged; it switches faster than a solenoid and allows closely spaced injections.
Dividing one injection event into pilot, main and post pulses to control ignition delay, noise, NOx and soot.
Pressure at which the spring-loaded needle lifts off its seat and fuel flow begins.
Nozzle whose spray comes from one or more drilled holes in the tip, giving fine atomisation and long penetration.
Nozzle with a flattened pin that changes spray direction and speed with needle lift, used to soften early injection.
Rapid opening and closing of the needle seen on a nozzle tester, taken as a sign of correct seating and free movement.
Small fall in engine speed from no load to full load in a governed engine, caused by the need for a finite sleeve movement.
Governor in which the venturi vacuum of the intake air acts on a diaphragm to move the fuel rack, used on small petrol engines.
Crank angle for which the primary circuit stays closed and current builds in the coil before the spark.
Two-winding induction coil whose primary current collapse induces a high secondary voltage across the plug gap.
Resistor in series with the primary winding that limits running current and is bypassed during cranking for a stronger spark.
Air gap between the centre and earth electrodes, typically 0.8 to 1.1 mm, which sets the voltage needed to spark.
Piezoelectric accelerometer bolted to the block that detects the characteristic vibration of knock so the ECU can retard spark.
